paragraphs.heading: The deepest known point
paragraphs.text: The Challenger Deep is the deepest known point of Earth's seabed. It lies in the western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench, in ocean territory of the Federated States of Micronesia. A 2021 study put its depth at 10,935 ± 6 m. The nearest land is Fais Island, 287 km to the southwest, with Guam 304 km to the northeast.

paragraphs.heading: Three basins in a row
paragraphs.text: It is a fairly small, slot-shaped dip in the floor of a much larger crescent-shaped trench. It is made of three basins in a staggered line from west to east, each 6 to 10 km long, 2 km wide and more than 10,840 m deep, with mounds 200 to 300 m higher between them. Sonar has recorded depths over 10,920 m in the western and eastern basins, while the center one is a little shallower. Sonar mapping in June 2020, together with crewed dives, showed slopes and piles of rock rising above a bed of pelagic ooze.

paragraphs.heading: Name and visitors
paragraphs.text: The deep is named after two British Royal Navy survey ships. HMS Challenger first located it on its 1872–1876 expedition, and HMS Challenger II established its record depth in 1950–1952. The first vehicle ever to go down was the US Navy bathyscaphe Trieste, in January 1960. By July 2022, 27 people had made the descent.

paragraphs.heading: A fish, or not
paragraphs.text: On the 1960 dive, the Trieste crew saw that the floor was diatomaceous ooze and reported a flatfish like a sole, about 30 cm long and 15 cm wide. In one crew member's telling, the floodlight on it was the first true light ever to reach those depths. Many marine biologists now doubt the sighting. They suggest it may have been a sea cucumber, which lives at such depths and could be mistaken for a sole.

paragraphs.heading: What lives there
paragraphs.text: Probes sent down have spotted more. The Kaiko probe's camera saw a sea cucumber, a scale worm and a shrimp, and the Nereus probe saw one polychaete worm, a many-legged predator about an inch long. Sediment collected by Kaiko held large numbers of simple organisms, mostly soft-shelled foraminifera. Eighty-five per cent were organic, soft-shelled allogromiids, an unusual share: in sediment from other deep-sea places, organic-walled forms make up 5% to 20%.

paragraphs.heading: Why soft shells
paragraphs.text: Tiny creatures with hard calcium carbonate shells struggle at extreme depth, because that material dissolves easily in high-pressure water. Scientists think the soft-shelled life may date from a time when the Challenger Deep was shallower. Over six to nine million years, as it sank to today's depth, many species died out or could not adapt to the rising pressure. In 2013, researchers also reported data suggesting that microbes thrive there.

paragraphs.heading: Pinning down the depth
paragraphs.text: A University of New Hampshire team split the history of measuring attempts into three groups: single-beam echo sounders of the 1950s to 1970s, early multibeam sounders from the 1980s, and modern high-resolution multibeam systems from after GPS. When more than two million soundings from a 2010 survey were analysed, the deepest point recorded in that mapping came out at 10,984 m. Even with the best 2010 equipment, the depth still carried an uncertainty of ±25 m.
